docs.title: gopantic
docs.text:
Parse JSON or YAML into a Go struct, convert what can be converted exactly, and run the rules in its validate tags, in one call. You get back the value the input meant, or an error.

type User struct {
    ID    int    `json:"id" validate:"required,min=1"`
    Name  string `json:"name" validate:"required,min=2"`
    Email string `json:"email" validate:"required,email"`
}

user, err := model.ParseInto[User]([]byte(`{"id": "42", "name": "Alice", "email": "alice@example.com"}`))
// user.ID == 42

The string "42" becomes the int 42 because that conversion loses nothing. "42.5" wouldn't fit an int, so it's an error. The same struct reads YAML with no other change.

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text:
gopantic suits code that reads input it doesn't control: API payloads where numbers arrive as strings, config files that may be JSON or YAML, data imports. You write one struct and get decoding, conversion and validation together, with every problem reported at once.

If your input is already well typed and JSON only, use encoding/json with go-playground/validator. It has far more rules, and you wouldn't be using what gopantic adds. The two are within 30% of each other on correctly typed JSON, so speed won't decide it. Input that needs converting takes about 3 times as long; see Benchmarks.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
go get github.com/1mb-dev/gopantic

Requires Go 1.24 or later. The one dependency is gopkg.in/yaml.v3.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: Start with Getting started. The Validation and Coercion guides are the two pages you will return to. Known limitations lists what gopantic doesn't do, and the changelog lists what v1.5.0 changed.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
All the code is one package, pkg/model:

File Holds parse.go ParseInto, Validate, the validation walk decode.go The type-directed walker and field tables coerce.go Scalar conversion validate.go Tags, the registry, per-type rule analysis validators.go Built-in rules format.go Format detection, depth checks cache.go CachedParser errors.go, config.go Error types, limits

docs.title: Decoding
docs.text:
JSON tries the fast path first. A byte scan checks the depth limit, then json.Unmarshal decodes straight into T. If that works, nothing else in the decoder runs, so correctly typed input costs little more than encoding/json.

When the decoder rejects a value, the input is decoded again by the walker. It builds a tree of raw byte ranges, then walks the target type, not the input. Each leaf goes to the standard decoder first, and coercion only sees what that decoder refused. So a json.RawMessage keeps its bytes and an UnmarshalJSON method runs, whether or not some other field needed coercion.

YAML always takes the walker, because yaml.v3 ignores json tags and decoding straight into T would drop those fields. yaml.v3 enforces its alias limits only on a whole-document decode, so one runs first and its result goes unused, except for the depth check.

A differential test compares each parse with encoding/json or yaml.v3, with and without a field that forces coercion. Fuzzing does the same on generated input.

docs.title: Validating
docs.text:
Every parse and every Validate goes through one walk, in parse.go. There is only one so that the rules that run can't depend on how a value was decoded.

Rules are parsed once per type and cached. That pass looks only at types, and records two things across everything reachable: tags that can't run, and whether any rule exists. So a typo fails under an empty slice, and a type with no rules skips the walk.

Paths for errors are built only when an error needs one. Building them as the walk descends would copy every enclosing map key once per element, and one long key above a large slice would turn that quadratic.

docs.title: Choices
docs.text:
ParseInto[User] returns a User, with no build step and no interface{} to assert. Code generators are faster, and that's the cost of having none.

Rules live on the struct, so they can't drift from it. A tag is a short string, though, which is why anything complicated becomes a registered function.

Coercion exists to accept input that means something obvious, and it stops where the meaning stops. An int8 can't hold 300, and returning 44 would be worse than failing. A misspelled tag is an error for the same reason: a rule that silently does nothing is a bug you can't see.

A parse reports every error it finds, so a client can fix them in one round. The cap of 100 is there because one error per element would otherwise let a large input allocate without limit.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
Measured on 2026-11-01 at commit 86e26f1, with Go 1.27.3 on an Intel Core i5-8257U at 1.40 GHz under macOS. Each figure is the median of three runs, and runs of the same benchmark differed by up to 20%. Treat differences smaller than that as ties.

The small struct has four fields and nine rules. The complex one adds a nested struct and a list of addresses, for 18 rules.

docs.title: Correctly typed JSON, parsed and validated
docs.text:
gopantic encoding/json + validator Small struct 2,275 ns, 10 allocs 2,596 ns, 10 allocs Complex struct 6,701 ns, 29 allocs 5,224 ns, 19 allocs

These are close enough that speed should not decide between them. gopantic allocates more memory on both: 453 bytes against 186 on the small struct, and 1,526 against 520 on the complex one.

docs.title: What the extras cost
docs.text:
These use the small struct, against 2,275 ns for correctly typed JSON.

Input Time Cost Numbers sent as strings 6,958 ns 3.1x YAML 18,639 ns 8.4x (against 2,230 ns for JSON through the same call)

Coercion is the expensive path because the whole input is decoded a second time by the walker. One string in a number field costs the same as several. YAML always takes that path.

docs.title: Validation alone
docs.text:
Validate on a struct already in memory, against validator's Struct.

gopantic validator Small struct 1,218 ns 1,615 ns Complex struct 2,941 ns 2,207 ns

docs.title: Caching
docs.text: For the same input, a parse took 2,982 ns and a cache hit 692 ns, about 4x less. A hit on this struct allocates once. A struct holding slices or maps pays to copy them on every hit, so its gain is smaller. See the caching guide.

docs.title: Hostile input
docs.text:
From tests/adversarial_bench_test.go. Each input needs coercion, so each goes through the walker.

Input Time 20,000 array items 40 ms 50,000 unknown keys 24 ms Nesting 30 levels deep 69 µs

docs.title: Running them
docs.text:
go test -run='^$' -bench=. -benchmem ./tests/
cd benchmarks && go test -run='^$' -bench=. -benchmem ./...

The comparisons against validator live in benchmarks/, a separate module, so that validator stays out of your dependency graph.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.

The format is based on Keep a Changelog, and this project adheres to Semantic Versioning.

A value gopantic returns without error is now the value the input meant, and every rule on a field either decoder can set has run. So input that v1.4 accepted can fail. If you need time to adapt, stay on v1.4.1 and work through Behavior changes below. Each item says what you will see and what to do, and names the row in tests/contract_test.go that holds it.

docs.title: Behavior changes
docs.text:
Input that used to pass can now be rejected, depending on the data:

  • Rules run on elements and values. v1.4 skipped rules on slice elements, array elements, map values and top-level slices on some paths. You will see validation errors on data that passed before. Fix the data or loosen the rule. Tests: validation/[]struct elements, validation/map[string]struct elements, validation/top-level []struct.
  • Rules run on every parse. v1.4 could stop checking nested structs for the rest of the process after the first parse of a type. You will see errors that came and went before. Tests: validation/nested rule, second parse, validation/pointer rule, second parse.
  • Numbers must fit. 300 into an int8, 4.7 into an int and -1 into a uint used to wrap, truncate or pass. They're now parse errors, in fields, slices, arrays and pointers, and in YAML as well as JSON. Use a wider type, or a float if fractions are real. Tests: the numeric group, and numeric/YAML float does not truncate into an int.
  • Unix timestamps must fall in years 1 to 9999. 1e300 and YAML .nan into a time.Time used to give a garbage date. Tests: numeric/time rejects a huge number, numeric/time rejects YAML NaN.
  • json.Number must hold a number. {"n":"abc"} used to store abc. YAML keeps the digits as written, and spellings only YAML has, like 0x10, store their value. Tests: numeric/an invalid json.Number is rejected, numeric/a YAML json.Number keeps its digits.
  • Floats at or past 2^53 no longer convert to integers. 1e16 into an int errors. Send the digits. Test: numeric/exponent integer past 2^53 rejected.
  • "NaN" and "Inf" no longer convert to floats. Send a number, or take a string field. Tests: numeric/string NaN rejected, numeric/string Inf rejected.
  • Objects no longer convert to strings. v1.4 returned Go syntax such as map[a:1]. Use a struct, a map or json.RawMessage. Test: numeric/object is not a string.

  • Rules past 32 levels of nesting are errors. v1.4 skipped the limit on inputs that needed coercion. A rule that deep now fails rather than going unchecked; raise it with SetMaxValidationDepth. Types with no rules aren't affected. Test: validation/rule below the depth limit fails closed.

  • Large YAML mappings can be refused. A document needing more than 50,000,000 key comparisons now errors before decoding: one mapping of 10,000 keys, or 100 of 1,000. Raise it with SetMaxYAMLKeyComparisons, or pass 0 to turn the budget off. Test: TestYAMLGuardChargesAllComparisons.

  • Some YAML keys are now errors. A null key can't go in a typed map, and a key that appears with two types through a merge can't go in an interface-keyed map. Both used to store the wrong thing. A null key on a struct is still ignored like any unknown key. Tests: yaml/a null key cannot go in a string map, yaml/merged keys of two types cannot share an interface map.

Types that used to work can now fail on every parse:

  • A tag that can't run is an error, for every parse and Validate of that type, even under an empty slice. This covers misspelled rules, a missing or malformed parameter such as min or min=abc, and stray commas. Rules that were never built in are the likely surprise: older docs showed gtfield as a feature, and it never existed. eqfield and oneof appeared as custom rules to register, so they fail only if you copied the tag without the registration. Register the rule or remove the tag. Use ParseValidationTags(...).TagErrors to find these in a test. Tests: the tags group.

  • Two fields claiming one YAML key is an error, as it is in yaml.v3. An inline struct is the usual cause. Test: yaml/two fields claiming one key is an error.

Validate can now fail where it passed:

  • Validate runs rules on json:"-" fields. v1.4 skipped them everywhere. Parsing still skips them when no decoder can set the field, but a field with json:"-" yaml:"x" keeps its rules on every parse, and required there now fails on JSON input. See Fields input cannot set. Tests: validation/Validate runs the rule on a json:"-" field, validation/input does not choose the format that skips a rule.

Values can change:

  • One field needing coercion no longer changes the others. v1.4 switched to a weaker decoder for the whole input, which lost json.RawMessage, UnmarshalJSON, embedded fields, exact large integers and case-insensitive keys. All of these now match encoding/json. Code that depended on the old results will see the correct ones. Tests: the divergence group.
  • Fixed arrays follow encoding/json when coercing: extra elements are dropped and missing ones are zero, where v1.4 returned an error. Use a slice with len=N to require a length. Test: seed 3bcd1ebd990ef103 under FuzzWalkerDifferential.
  • Absent slices stay nil, not empty, when coercing. Test: divergence/containers absent.
  • YAML keys are exact. username: no longer fills a field tagged json:"user_name". The key comes from the yaml tag, then the json tag, then the lowercased field name. Tests: yaml/json tag honoured without coercion, yaml/yaml tag honoured inside []struct.

Errors look different:

  • Field is the leaf name and FieldPath the full path, such as Name and Items[1].Name. Test: validation/FieldPath is the full path.
  • A parse reports at most 100 errors, then one saying it stopped. Test: validation/error count is capped on []struct.
  • ParseError messages leave out values of sensitive fields. Read SanitizedValue() or Value instead of parsing the message. Tests: the errors group.
  • A rejected object or array no longer sits in ParseError.Value. It holds "object" or "array", since a secret could be nested inside. Test: errors/a rejected object does not carry its contents.

CachedParser differs:

  • Results are copies. Code that relied on two callers sharing a slice, which was never safe, will no longer see it. Types holding references gopantic can't copy are parsed on every call. Tests: cache/mutating a hit does not reach the next caller, TestCachedParserBypassesUncopyableTypes.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• A small YAML document could exhaust memory or CPU. yaml.v3 compares every pair of keys and formats an error for each duplicate, so 15 KB of repeated keys allocated 800 MB and 1.2 MB of distinct keys took 2 minutes, far below MaxInputSize. ParseInto auto-detects YAML, so this reached endpoints that only expect JSON. Duplicates are now rejected in linear time and the remaining cost has a budget. Use ParseIntoWithFormat with FormatJSON for JSON-only input.
  • Validation could be skipped: nested rules stopped running after the first parse of a type, and rules on slice elements, map values and top-level slices didn't always run. Input that should have been rejected was returned as valid.
  • CachedParser returned shared slices and maps, so one caller could alter what the next received. Keys for input under 1 KB used a 64-bit FNV hash, which can be made to collide; they are now SHA-256.
  • Integers wrapped silently on overflow, so a limit checked after parsing could be passed with a value that wrapped into range.
  • ParseError messages quoted values of sensitive fields, and values of json:"-" fields reached ToJSON.
  • The YAML depth limit missed maps with non-string keys.
  • The validator registry had a data race under concurrent registration.

docs.title: Migration Notes
docs.text:
New recommended pattern for json.RawMessage fields:

type Request struct {
    Name        string          `json:"name" validate:"required"`

}

// Now works seamlessly

New standalone validation pattern:

var req Request
json.Unmarshal(body, &req)  // Use standard library
model.Validate(&req)         // Apply gopantic validation

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
go get github.com/1mb-dev/gopantic

Everything lives in one package, github.com/1mb-dev/gopantic/pkg/model.

docs.title: Parse
docs.text:
Describe the data as a struct. json tags name the keys, and validate tags hold the rules.

type User struct {
    ID       int    `json:"id" validate:"required,min=1"`
    Username string `json:"username" validate:"required,min=3,max=50"`
    Email    string `json:"email" validate:"required,email"`
    Age      int    `json:"age" validate:"min=0,max=150"`
}

data := []byte(`{"id": "123", "username": "alice", "email": "alice@example.com", "age": 25}`)

user, err := model.ParseInto[User](data)

ParseInto looks at the input to tell JSON from YAML, decodes it, converts values that need it, and validates the result. Here "123" became the int 123. The coercion guide lists what converts.

docs.title: YAML
docs.text:
The same struct and the same call work on YAML, and json tags apply to it too:

user, err := model.ParseInto[User]([]byte(`
id: 456
username: bob
email: bob@example.com
age: 30
`))

Detection reads the first byte, so { or [ always means JSON. If you know the format, say so, and do this on any endpoint that only expects JSON, since otherwise a client can send YAML:

user, err := model.ParseIntoWithFormat[User](data, model.FormatYAML)

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
A failed parse returns the zero value and an error covering every problem found, up to 100.

_, err := model.ParseInto[User]([]byte(`{"id": "x", "username": "al", "email": "alice@example.com"}`))
fmt.Println(err)
// multiple errors: parse error on field "ID": cannot parse string "x" as integer: ...;
// validation error on field "Username": string length must be at least 3 characters

To act on each problem, use errors.As for the first of a kind, or walk the list:

var list model.ErrorList
if errors.As(err, &list) {
    for _, v := range list.ValidationErrors() {
        fmt.Println(v.FieldPath, v.Rule) // Username min
    }
}

Error messages can quote the input. Values of sensitive fields are kept out, but don't send messages to clients.

docs.title: Validate without parsing
docs.text:
Validate runs the same rules on a struct you filled in yourself:

user := User{ID: 7, Username: "alice", Email: "alice@example.com"}
err := model.Validate(&user)

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Inputs over 10 MB, and input nested past 64 levels, are rejected before decoding. Rules stop at 32 levels of nested structs, with an error. All three can be changed:

model.SetMaxInputSize(5 * 1024 * 1024)
model.SetMaxStructureDepth(32)
model.SetMaxValidationDepth(16)

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The validation guide covers every rule and how to add your own. To parse the same bytes repeatedly, see caching.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text: Things gopantic doesn't do, or does differently from what you might assume. Most are deliberate. A few are costs accepted for now.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: gopkg.in/yaml.v3 is archived upstream and gets no more changes. It works, but a bug in it would mean moving to a maintained fork.

docs.title: Coercion
docs.text:
You can't turn it off. A string in a numeric field is converted if it can be, and the coercion guide shows what to do instead.

Floats at or past 2^53 are rejected for integer fields even when they look whole: 1e16 and 9007199254740992.0 both error, since a float that large may already have been rounded. Writing the digits out works, so send 10000000000000000.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
If you parse into a type with a rule on a json:"-" field and never call Validate, that rule doesn't run. See Fields input cannot set. Validate runs such a field's own rules but doesn't go inside it, so call Validate on the inner value if it needs checking.

required means not zero, so it can't tell a sent 0 from an absent key. Use a pointer.

Rules inside whatever an interface{} field holds don't run.

The built-in set is small. There's no url, uuid, oneof or gt, and unknown rules are errors, so anything else has to be registered.

A value with a real pointer loop, not tagged json:"-", stops at the depth limit with an error, though nothing is wrong with it.

An element that fails to decode can be reported twice: {"items":[5]} into a []Item gives the conversion error, and also a required error for the zero value. The same goes for a map key with more than one spelling, like "007" into a map[int]Item. No bad value gets through, but you may see an extra line.

docs.title: Formats
docs.text:
An inline map needs string keys: map[interface{}]T with yaml:",inline" errors on every key, as it does in yaml.v3.

Input starting with { or [ is treated as JSON, so one-line YAML like {a: 1} is a syntax error under ParseInto. Use ParseIntoWithFormat with FormatYAML.

A YAML document can't need more than 50,000,000 key comparisons, because yaml.v3 compares every pair of keys in a mapping, and again for each alias of it. That's one mapping of 10,000 keys, or 100 of 1,000. SetMaxYAMLKeyComparisons changes it.

YAML always takes the slow path through the walker, because yaml.v3 ignores json tags. Benchmarks has the cost.

docs.title: Sensitive values
docs.text:
Matching is by substring on names. It over-redacts Author, and it can't know Hash is secret unless the field is tagged json:"-" or you add a pattern.

Long map keys match on their first 64 bytes, because scanning whole keys would let one long key cost time on every error. A key that only looks sensitive past that point isn't redacted.

Errors keep the rejected value in Value. Log SanitizedValue().

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
MaxEntries counts entries. There's no memory limit, and eviction scans the whole cache, which is fine at the default of 1000 and slower far past it.

A hit copies through reflection, so the saving shrinks as a type holds more slices and maps. A large map[string]any can take almost as long to copy as to parse, and allocate as much.

Only time.Time is treated as immutable. Other types holding hidden pointers aren't cached, even when sharing them would be safe.

A hit skips validation; see Keys and staleness.

docs.title: Coming from encoding/json and validator
docs.text:
Upgrading from an older gopantic instead? The v1.5.0 changelog lists what changed.

The usual code:

var user User
if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &user); err != nil {
    return User{}, err
}
if err := validate.Struct(user); err != nil {
    return User{}, err
}
return user, nil

becomes:

return model.ParseInto[User](data)

Your structs keep their json tags. Three things need attention: the validate tags, fields your code fills in, and error handling.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
gopantic has fewer rules than validator, and an unknown one is an error on every parse, so you will find out at once.

validator gopantic required, min, max, len, email, alpha, alphanum The same names, with the differences below dive Remove it. Rules on elements and map values always run omitempty Remove it, and register a rule that accepts empty input if you need one eqfield, gtfield, nefield, oneof, url, uuid, others Not built in. Register your own

required differs for pointers: validator and gopantic both fail a nil pointer, and gopantic passes a pointer to a zero value. Validator's email is stricter in places, and gopantic's is a format check, not a full RFC parser.

docs.title: Fields your code fills in
docs.text:
With validator, this runs on whatever the struct holds when you call it:

KBID string `json:"-" validate:"required"`

ParseInto validates during the parse, before your code has set KBID, so it skips that rule. Keep the tag and call model.Validate after filling the field in. Fields input cannot set has the details, and this is the one place where dropping the second call would silently lose a check.

docs.title: Coercion
docs.text: gopantic accepts {"age": "25"} for an int, where encoding/json errors. If your API should reject that, keep json.Unmarshal and call model.Validate on its result. You keep the same rules and the strict decoder.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
// validator
var errs validator.ValidationErrors
if errors.As(err, &errs) {
    for _, e := range errs {
        fmt.Println(e.Field(), e.Tag())
    }
}

// gopantic
var list model.ErrorList
if errors.As(err, &list) {
    for _, e := range list.ValidationErrors() {
        fmt.Println(e.FieldPath, e.Rule)
    }
}

A list can also hold *model.ParseError for values that could not be converted.

docs.title: Custom rules
docs.text:
// validator
validate.RegisterValidation("strong", func(fl validator.FieldLevel) bool {
    return isStrong(fl.Field().String())
})

// gopantic
model.RegisterGlobalFunc("strong", func(field string, value interface{}, params map[string]interface{}) error {
    if s, ok := value.(string); ok && !isStrong(s) {
        return model.NewValidationError(field, value, "strong", "password is too weak")
    }
    return nil
})

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
CachedParser remembers the result for each exact input. It helps when the same bytes arrive again: a config file read on every reload, a retried request, a redelivered queue message. If each input is different, it costs a hash per call and returns nothing.

parser := model.NewCachedParser[Config](nil)
defer parser.Close()

config, err := parser.Parse(data) // parses
config, err = parser.Parse(data)  // same bytes: returned from the cache

A parser holds one type and is safe for concurrent use, so create one and share it. Only successful parses are cached. Close stops the background cleanup and can be called more than once.

docs.title: Results are copies
docs.text:
Each caller gets its own copy, so changing a returned slice or map can't affect the cache or anyone else. That copy is the price of a hit: a struct of plain values costs nothing extra, while one holding slices and maps pays to copy them each time.

A type holding references gopantic can't copy, such as an unexported slice, a *big.Int or a netip.Addr, is parsed on every call, and Stats shows a hit rate of zero. So is a value nested past 1,024 levels of copying.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parser := model.NewCachedParser[Config](&model.CacheConfig{
    TTL:             5 * time.Minute,
    MaxEntries:      100,
    CleanupInterval: time.Minute,
})
Field Default Meaning TTL 1 hour How long an entry lives MaxEntries 1000 Entries kept; the oldest goes first CleanupInterval 30 minutes How often expired entries are swept; 0 turns the sweep off

MaxEntries counts entries, not bytes. A cache of large documents holds that many large documents. An entry is evicted by age, whether or not it's still being hit.

docs.title: Checking it helps
docs.text:
size, maxSize, hitRate := parser.Stats()

A low hit rate means the inputs aren't repeating, and a plain ParseInto will serve you better. ClearCache empties the cache.

docs.title: Keys and staleness
docs.text:
The key is a SHA-256 of the input plus its format, so one changed byte is a different entry. A hit doesn't run validation again. If you replace a validator under an existing name, entries already cached keep the old verdict until they expire or you call ClearCache.

The benchmarks show what a hit saves.

docs.title: Coercion
docs.text: gopantic hands input to the standard decoder first. Only when that decoder rejects a value does coercion look at it, and it converts the value only if nothing is lost. Input that needs no conversion is decoded exactly as encoding/json or yaml.v3 would decode it, and one field needing conversion doesn't change how the others decode.

docs.title: What converts
docs.text:
Into From Example Integer kinds Number strings, whole floats "42" and 42.0 to 42 Floats Number strings, integers "3.14" to 3.14 bool The strings below, numbers "yes" to true, 0 to false string Numbers, booleans 42 to "42", true to "true" time.Time Date strings, Unix seconds 1704067200

The strings accepted as booleans are true, 1, yes, on and false, 0, no, off, in lower, title or upper case. The empty string is false.

Times parse as RFC 3339, 2006-01-02T15:04:05, 2006-01-02 15:04:05 or 2006-01-02. Unix seconds have to fall in years 1 to 9999.

The rules are the same inside slices, arrays, pointers and map values, and in map keys, so map[int]string reads {"1": "a"}.

docs.title: What errors
docs.text:
Coercion refuses anything that would change the value:

Input Target Why 300 int8 Out of range 4.7 int Fractional -1 uint Negative 1e60 float32 Out of range 1e16 int Written as a float at or past 2^53, so it may have been rounded already "NaN", "Inf" Any float Not a number gopantic will return {"a": 1} string Would hand back Go syntax as if it were the input 1e300 time.Time Past year 9999 abc json.Number Not a number

Whole numbers written out in full are read digit by digit, so 9007199254740993 stays exact in an int64. The rules are the same in YAML, where yaml.v3 alone would turn 1.9 into 1. A json.Number keeps the digits as written.

docs.title: Types that decode themselves
docs.text: Fields with an UnmarshalJSON, UnmarshalYAML or UnmarshalText method decode themselves, and json.RawMessage keeps its bytes as they arrived. Coercion leaves them alone, with one exception: time.Time falls back to the wider list of formats above.

docs.title: Coercion cannot be turned off
docs.text:
If a string in a numeric field should be an error, gopantic is the wrong tool for that field. Decode with encoding/json, then call model.Validate:

var req Request
if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &req); err != nil {
    return err
}
err := model.Validate(&req)

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Rules go in a validate tag, separated by commas. All of them run, and all failures are reported.

type User struct {
    Name  string `json:"name" validate:"required,min=2,max=50"`
    Email string `json:"email" validate:"required,email"`
}

docs.title: Built-in rules
docs.text:
Rule Meaning required Not the zero value min=N, max=N Bounds on a number, or on the length of a string, slice or array length=N, or len=N Exact length of a string, slice or array email Looks like an email address alpha Letters a to z only alphanum Letters and digits only

String lengths count bytes. An empty string fails required and passes min=0, and required can't tell an absent 0 from a sent one. Use a pointer when that matters:

Age *int `json:"age" validate:"required"` // nil fails, 0 passes

docs.title: Where rules apply
docs.text:
Rules run wherever the type holds them: nested structs, pointers, the elements of slices and arrays, map values, and top-level slices and maps. So model.ParseInto[[]User](data) checks every user.

type Order struct {
    Items []Item          `json:"items"` // each Item is validated
    Meta  map[string]Item `json:"meta"`  // each value is validated
}

Errors from nested values carry the full path in FieldPath, such as Items[1].Name, and the leaf name in Field.

docs.title: A tag that cannot run is an error
docs.text:
A misspelled rule would otherwise leave a field unchecked with no sign of it. So an unknown rule, a missing or malformed parameter, or a stray comma fails every parse and every Validate for that type, even when the input never reaches the field:

main.Order.Name: invalid validate tag "requird": unknown validator "requird":
use one of alpha, alphanum, email, len, length, max, min, required, or register it first

This also catches rules copied from go-playground/validator that gopantic doesn't have. Register those yourself, as below.

docs.title: Your own rules
docs.text:
Register a function under a name, then use the name in tags. Do this before parsing, or at any point: registering clears the cached rules, so types parsed earlier pick it up.

model.RegisterGlobalFunc("is_even", func(field string, value interface{}, params map[string]interface{}) error {
    if n, ok := value.(int); ok && n%2 != 0 {
        return model.NewValidationError(field, value, "is_even", "must be even")
    }
    return nil
})

type Numbers struct {
    Count int `json:"count" validate:"is_even"`
}

The text after = arrives as params["value"], a float64 if it reads as a number and a string otherwise:

model.RegisterGlobalFunc("oneof", func(field string, value interface{}, params map[string]interface{}) error {
    allowed, _ := params["value"].(string)
    for _, option := range strings.Fields(allowed) {
        if value == option {
            return nil
        }
    }
    return model.NewValidationError(field, value, "oneof", "must be one of: "+allowed)
})

type Post struct {
    Status string `json:"status" validate:"oneof=draft published archived"`
}

To compare fields, register a cross-field rule, which also receives the struct:

model.RegisterGlobalCrossFieldFunc("eqfield", func(field string, value interface{}, parent reflect.Value, params map[string]interface{}) error {
    other := parent.FieldByName(params["value"].(string))
    if !other.IsValid() || other.Interface() != value {
        return model.NewValidationError(field, value, "eqfield", "fields do not match")
    }
    return nil
})

type Registration struct {
    Password string `json:"password" validate:"required,min=8"`
    Confirm  string `json:"confirm" validate:"required,eqfield=Password"`
}

docs.title: Fields input cannot set
docs.text:
A field tagged json:"-" is often filled in by your code, from a URL parameter or a session. A parse can't set it, so a parse doesn't check it. Call Validate once you have:

type CreateChat struct {
    Message string `json:"message" validate:"required"`
    KBID    string `json:"-" validate:"required"`
}

req, err := model.ParseInto[CreateChat](body) // KBID is not checked here
if err != nil {
    return err
}
req.KBID = kbIDFromPath(r)
err = model.Validate(&req) // now it is

The rule is the same for any field: a parse skips rules on fields neither decoder can set, and Validate runs them. Whether a field can be set doesn't depend on which format arrived, so a field with json:"-" yaml:"x" keeps its rules on JSON input too, and required there fails every JSON parse.

Validate runs a field's own rules but doesn't go inside such a field. A Parent *Node tagged json:"-" is usually a way back up a tree, and it may point at a type from another library. To check what is inside, call Validate on that value.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
A failed parse returns a model.ErrorList, which works with errors.As:

var v *model.ValidationError
if errors.As(err, &v) {
    fmt.Println(v.FieldPath, v.Rule, v.Message)
}

errors.As stops at the first match. list.ValidationErrors() returns them all, list.GroupByField() groups them, and list.ToJSON() renders a report you can return from an API. Conversion failures are *model.ParseError. A parse reports at most 100 errors and then one saying it stopped.

docs.title: Sensitive values
docs.text:
Errors keep the rejected value in their Value field, or "object" or "array" in place of a rejected container, since a secret could sit inside one. SanitizedValue() returns [REDACTED] instead when the field is sensitive, and ToJSON uses it. A ParseError on a sensitive field also leaves the value out of its message, which would otherwise quote it.

A field is sensitive when it, or anything above it, has a Go name or input key containing password, passwd, secret, token, key, credential, auth, api_key, apikey, private or bearer, or is tagged json:"-". The match ignores case and looks anywhere in the name, so Author and Monkey count too. Change the list with model.SetSensitiveFieldPatterns or model.AddSensitiveFieldPattern.

Log SanitizedValue(), never Value.

docs.title: API
docs.text: This page groups the package by job. pkg.go.dev has every symbol.

docs.title: Parsing
docs.text:
func ParseInto[T any](raw []byte) (T, error)
func ParseIntoWithFormat[T any](raw []byte, format Format) (T, error)
func DetectFormat(raw []byte) Format

T can be a struct, a pointer, a slice, an array or a map. On error the returned value is the zero value. format is FormatJSON or FormatYAML. DetectFormat calls input starting with { or [ JSON, and otherwise looks for YAML markers, falling back to JSON.

docs.title: Validating
docs.text:
func Validate[T any](v *T) error

Runs the rules on a struct you already hold. Unlike a parse, it also runs the rules on fields no decoder can set; see Fields input cannot set.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
func RegisterGlobalFunc(name string, fn ValidatorFunc)
func RegisterGlobalCrossFieldFunc(name string, fn CrossFieldValidatorFunc)
func GetDefaultRegistry() *ValidatorRegistry
func ParseValidationTags(typ reflect.Type) *StructValidation
func ClearValidationCache()

type ValidatorFunc func(fieldName string, value interface{}, params map[string]interface{}) error
type CrossFieldValidatorFunc func(fieldName string, fieldValue interface{}, structValue reflect.Value, params map[string]interface{}) error

Registering on the default registry, by these functions or its own Register, RegisterFunc and RegisterCrossFieldFunc methods, is safe at any time and clears cached rules. ClearValidationCache is only needed if something else changed a type's rules, which ordinary code doesn't do.

ParseValidationTags returns the rules for a type. Its TagErrors field lists the tags that can't run, for this type and every type it reaches, so a test can fail on them before any input arrives:

func TestTags(t *testing.T) {
    if errs := model.ParseValidationTags(reflect.TypeOf(Order{})).TagErrors; len(errs) > 0 {
        t.Fatal(errs)
    }
}

docs.title: Coercing one value
docs.text:
func CoerceValue(value interface{}, target reflect.Type, fieldName string) (interface{}, error)
func CoerceValueWithFormat(value interface{}, target reflect.Type, fieldName string, format Format) (interface{}, error)

Applies the coercion rules to a single value. Integer kinds come back as int64 or uint64, and floats as float64, checked against the range of target.

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
func NewCachedParser[T any](config *CacheConfig) *CachedParser[T]
func DefaultCacheConfig() *CacheConfig

func (cp *CachedParser[T]) Parse(data []byte) (T, error)
func (cp *CachedParser[T]) ParseWithFormat(data []byte, format Format) (T, error)
func (cp *CachedParser[T]) Stats() (size, maxSize int, hitRate float64)
func (cp *CachedParser[T]) ClearCache()
func (cp *CachedParser[T]) Close()

See the caching guide.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
type ParseError struct {
    Field, Type, Message string
    Value                interface{}
}

type ValidationError struct {
    Field     string // Leaf name: "Name"
    FieldPath string // Full path: "Items[1].Name"
    Value     interface{}
    Rule      string
    Message   string
    Details   map[string]interface{}
}

Both have SanitizedValue(). A failed parse or Validate returns an ErrorList holding them, plus plain errors for tags that can't run or a depth limit. ErrorList works with errors.As and errors.Is, and has ValidationErrors, GroupByField, ToStructuredReport and ToJSON. Syntax errors and oversized input come back as plain errors.

Custom rules build their errors with NewValidationError, or NewValidationErrorWithDetails to attach Details.

docs.title: Limits and settings
docs.text:
Setting Default Meaning SetMaxInputSize 10 MB Larger input is rejected; 0 turns the check off SetMaxStructureDepth 64 Deeper input is rejected; 0 turns the check off SetMaxYAMLKeyComparisons 50,000,000 YAML needing more key comparisons is rejected; 0 turns the budget off SetMaxValidationDepth 32 Rules reached deeper than this are an error SetMaxCacheSize 1000 Types whose rules stay cached; 0 is unlimited

Each has a matching getter. They are safe for concurrent use. The package variables of the same names aren't, so use these.

SetSensitiveFieldPatterns, AddSensitiveFieldPattern, GetSensitiveFieldPatterns and IsSensitiveField control sensitive values.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
Anything encoding/json decodes, gopantic decodes the same way. These are the cases worth knowing.

Type Behaviour Numbers, strings, booleans Decoded, then coerced if the decoder refused time.Time RFC 3339, plus the other formats in the coercion guide and Unix seconds Structs, pointers Rules inside them run. A nil pointer has nothing to check Slices, arrays Rules run on each element map[K]V Rules run on each value. K can be a string or an integer, and interface{} for YAML, which keeps the key's type interface{} Holds what the decoder produced. required works, and nothing goes inside it json.RawMessage Keeps its bytes as they arrived Types with UnmarshalJSON, UnmarshalYAML or UnmarshalText Decode themselves. validate tags still apply to them

docs.title: Absent, null and zero
docs.text:
A plain field can't tell an absent key from a zero value. A pointer can:

type Update struct {
    Name *string `json:"name"` // nil: not sent. "": sent empty
    Age  *int    `json:"age"`
}

An absent or null slice is nil, and [] is empty and not nil, as with encoding/json.

docs.title: Fixed arrays
docs.text:
Arrays follow encoding/json: extra elements are dropped and missing ones stay zero, with no error. To require a length, use a slice and a rule:

Scores []float64 `json:"scores" validate:"len=3"`

docs.title: Struct tags
docs.text:
json tags work as in encoding/json, including json:"-" and omitempty, embedded structs, and case-insensitive key matching. A key that matches no field is ignored.

For YAML, a field's key comes from its yaml tag, then its json tag, then its lowercased name. yaml:",inline" and merge keys behave as in yaml.v3. A field with json:"-" and no yaml tag is skipped on YAML too.

type Config struct {
    Host string `json:"host"`            // key "host" in both
    Port int    `yaml:"port" json:"p"`   // "port" in YAML, "p" in JSON
    TLS  bool                             // key "tls" in YAML, any case of "TLS" in JSON
}

docs.title: Trees and cycles
docs.text:
A type can refer to itself, and input is a tree, so nothing loops. Validate on a value you built with a real cycle stops at the depth limit with an error. Tag a back-pointer json:"-" and Validate won't follow it:

type Node struct {
    Name     string  `json:"name" validate:"required"`
    Children []*Node `json:"children"`
    Parent   *Node   `json:"-"`
}
